protestant-dry-democratic-nominee.summary: In this world, the voters I interviewed lean 9.0 points further toward Smith than the same people did in 1928 as it was. Smith wins, 311–220. The closest call is Nebraska, which holds for Hoover by 3.4 points. Smith wins in 100 of 100 draws. Extremely low confidence. The interviews point the other way from the historical record.
assumptions: The out-party nominee's Catholicism and wet stance no longer drive voters. Religious and Prohibition-based defection and turnout shift toward the 1928 baseline for a generic party candidate, and Prohibition no longer separates the parties.
howIGotThis: What changed: The party out of the presidency since 1921 is led by a Protestant who backs Prohibition, so neither religion nor liquor divides the two candidates.

What historians found (10 findings, strong evidence): No source models a Protestant dry Democratic nominee. Real 1928 evidence, with a Catholic wet Smith, shows large Southern losses and Catholic urban gains, with scholars split on whether religion or prosperity drove the result. Nothing separates religion from liquor numerically.
The numbers: the 1920 and 1930 census counts interpolated to 1928 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1928 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
Extremely low confidence: The interviews point the other way from the historical record. 4 of 12 people interviewed took the news to be about the other candidate; their answers were left out.

findings.claim: Smith's Catholicism, opposition to Prohibition and New York machine ties cost him support, especially among rural voters.
Democrats picked Protestant dry Robinson as running mate to ease Southern fears, but the South still defected.
Hoover won 58.2% of the popular vote and 444 electoral votes; Smith won 40.8% and 87.

caveats: No source models a Protestant dry Democratic nominee; all evidence is from the real Catholic wet Smith.
Religion, liquor, Tammany and prosperity moved together and cannot be separated.
No breakdowns by sex, citizenship, race, border states or West; no evidence on dry voters when both parties backed Prohibition.

before.quote: The Republican has done right by business and kept us from hard times. I'll stick with the administration's man tomorrow.
before.reason: Fred Johnson is a 63-year-old white male born in the United States, eligible to vote in Kansas. As someone engaged in store or office work in a town, he would likely benefit from the prosperity credited to the current administration and would be cautious about the Socialist alternatives circulating in labor press he may have encountered.

after.quote: I'm going to vote tomorrow for the Democrat. The Republican hasn't done right by us farmers, and this fellow's got the right idea about enforcing the law and helping with the crops.
after.reason: Fred Johnson is a 63-year-old white man in Kansas eligible and likely to vote. Smith's strong pledge on Prohibition enforcement and farm relief appeals to his circumstances, though Hoover's policies offer a credible alternative.

before.quote: The fellow they've got running for the Democrats, he's Catholic—that's what folks keep saying bothers them. I'll stick with the Republican unless something changes by tomorrow.
before.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill worker in Massachusetts eligible to vote under the literacy test. The religious issue dominating the 1928 campaign—Catholic candidate Smith versus Protestant Republican Hoover—strongly influences working-class Protestant voters in New England. Reed's wage-dependent status makes him sensitive to both prohibition enforcement and farm/labor policies, but the religious question appears decisive in his community.

after.quote: Things are good now, better than they were. I'll stick with the fellow who's kept things steady, though the other man makes sense about looking after working people like us.
after.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill worker in Massachusetts during prosperity times, and both candidates support Prohibition, so religious and dry concerns do not sharply divide them. He likely favors the party in power that presides over current economic good times, though the opposition candidate's appeal to working men and criticism of monopoly creates some pull.

before.quote: The Republican talks sense about helping us farmers without the government getting too deep into business. That appeals to me more than breaking up what works.

She reads local newspapers about political issues and would have practical interest in the farm policies both candidates are discussing, particularly the pledges around farm surplus and price support, which directly affect her household's livelihood.

after.quote: The farm board idea sounds practical for us, and the Republican's been good enough on keeping things steady. Though I do wonder if the other fellow might help us more with the big outfits squeezing us smaller farmers.
after.reason: Helen lives in Indiana farm country where women have voted since 1919 and will be allowed to vote tomorrow. Both candidates pledge Prohibition enforcement, which matters to rural Protestant voters. Hoover's farm board and tariff protection directly address her household's farming concerns, while Smith's critique of current farm policy and monopolies appeals to her sense of fairness, though the sitting administration's prosperity narrative carries weight.

before.quote: I've heard tell that Mr. Hoover's kept things steady and prosperous these past years. That matters more to me than the other fellow's talk about breaking things up.
before.reason: Bertha Lawson is a woman who has had the right to vote in Mississippi since 1920, but literacy tests and poll taxes create real barriers to registration and voting, particularly in rural Mississippi. Her mill-worker household circumstances and the proximity of tomorrow's election suggest modest engagement, but uncertainty about whether she has cleared registration hurdles.

after.quote: The man from out West says he'll actually enforce the dry laws and help us farmers get a fair price. That matters more than talk.
after.reason: Bertha is a white woman in Mississippi legally able to vote since 1920, though poll taxes and literacy tests create barriers. The recent news about Prohibition enforcement and farming policy, particularly criticism of the incumbent's weak enforcement record, aligns with Democratic Smith's messaging on both fronts.

before.quote: I'll be voting for the Republican. The farm board sounds like real help for us, and these tariffs could steady prices without the government getting into farming itself. That's the sensible approach.
before.reason: Fred Johnson is a farmer in rural New York in 1928, and the incumbent Republican administration's farm board proposal and tariff protection directly address agricultural concerns that dominate his livelihood. He has encountered recent local news about Prohibition enforcement efforts and the religious controversy around the Democratic nominee, both matters his community appears to view unfavorably.

after.quote: I'm voting for the fellow who says government ought to help us farmers with these surpluses. The prices have been rough, and he sounds like he means it.
after.reason: Fred Johnson is a countryside farmer in New York who can vote. Recent news coverage of Prohibition enforcement and the Volstead Act reinforces the salience of this issue, and Q's platform on farm relief aligns with rural economic distress.

Smith's platform directly addresses crop surplus problems that harm farmer income, and both candidates pledge firm Prohibition enforcement, but Q's stronger dry support and anti-monopoly stance appeal more to a rural Protestant farmer of his era and region.

As a farmer's wife concerned with farm relief and living under Prohibition, she leans toward the opposition candidate's promises of agricultural intervention and stricter enforcement, though the sitting administration's farm board proposal and prosperity record give her some pause.

after.quote: The Republican's got the right idea about helping the farmers and breaking up the big money men. And he'll actually enforce the law, unlike that fellow they've got now.

Smith pledges intervention for farmers and action against monopolies, while also maintaining Prohibition enforcement that appeals to his Protestant values. The recent news about Hoover's weak enforcement record in New York as governor has raised doubts about his commitment to the liquor laws.

before.quote: The country's doing well enough as it is. I don't hold with voting a man down just for his religion, but I'm not ready to trade what's working for promises.
before.reason: William Robinson is a Texas storekeeper or office worker in 1928, living through Republican prosperity and supporting the party in power. The religious controversy swirling around the opposing candidate troubles him as a matter of principle, but he is not entirely settled.

after.quote: The farm situation is what matters most to me. Hoover's got the board plan that might help us get better prices for what we grow.
after.reason: William Robinson is a rural Texan in 1928 facing the farm economy crisis and the divisive religious question around the Catholic nominee Smith. The recent clippings emphasize warnings against voting on religious grounds while also showing real anti-Catholic anxiety in many Protestant sections of the country where few Catholics live—precisely Robinson's circumstance. His likely inclination is toward Hoover's Republican farm program and the safer Protestant choice, though genuine uncertainty lingers about voting primarily on religion.
